cases.title: Enterprise NFR Work Fabric
cases.subtitle: A strategic, operating-model, architecture, and experience blueprint for connected non-financial-risk work.
cases.problem: Large regulated organisations often have capable systems but fragmented work. Context, evidence, ownership, decisions, and actions break across handoffs, processes, meetings, email, and specialist tools.
cases.whyItMattered: Non-financial-risk work spans eight process families that share events, evidence and people. Treating each one as a separate AI use case repeats the build and keeps the fragmentation.
constraints: Systems of record stay authoritative. The fabric connects them and does not replace them.
Every view and every action is checked against role, case relationship and authority.
Process ownership stays federated. No single standard process is imposed on all disciplines.
No value numbers before a baseline exists in the organisation's own context.
The conversation it supports is introductory: it asks for no scope, funding or architecture decision.
cases.role: Author of the blueprint and product owner of the interactive experience: the thesis, process and work-object model, architecture, security and governance model, operating model, value framework and plan, and the acceptance tests the build had to pass.

contributions.detail: The work object as the unit of transformation, five ideas an executive audience should remember, and the guided story built around them.
Eight process families as one network, the process-module contract and the persistent work object.
Shared platform team, federated process owners, enterprise control partners and independent oversight, with a nine-step asset lifecycle.
Work, shared-service and control planes; Flow Engine, routing, evidence and semantics; systems-of-record boundaries.
Contextual access, separated read and action rights, bound approvals, controlled write-back and audit receipts.
Six value lenses, four cost lenses and cost per completed, controlled process as the unit measure.
A 22-scene guided story and 15 explorer deep dives, built with AI assistance from my specification and reviewed scene by scene.
An adoption decision for every library, with exact use, licence, bundle impact, risk and fallback recorded before installation.

contributions.area: Acceptance tests, accessibility, performance and QA
contributions.detail: 49 acceptance tests written before the build, end-to-end and accessibility checks on every route, and Lighthouse budgets.

decisions.title: Transform the work object, not another application
decisions.rationale: Context survives a handover only if something persistent carries it. Applications change; the case, review or incident is what people actually work on.

decisions.title: Derive the process network from source data
decisions.rationale: Processes, steps and links are imported from a reference dataset at a pinned commit, so the network is data rather than a drawing. ORM and RCSA emerge as the hubs.

decisions.title: Work moves horizontally; services and controls run vertically
decisions.rationale: Identity, security and governance are platform primitives every process uses, not features rebuilt for each use case.

decisions.title: Read before write, cluster before scale
decisions.rationale: Write-back comes only after read, context, approval and recovery patterns are proven. Expansion follows process clusters with the most shared capability.

decisions.title: Federated ownership with a shared platform team
decisions.rationale: The platform team does not own every process, and process owners do not rebuild shared infrastructure.

architecture.label: Work plane
architecture.detail: Work objects, process modules, roles, evidence, decisions, actions and monitoring.

architecture.label: Shared service plane
architecture.detail: Flow Engine, queues and routing, intelligence, evidence and semantics, integration and observability.

architecture.label: Control and management plane
architecture.detail: Contextual identity, authority and segregation, evaluation, governance lifecycle, release management and the Control Tower.

architecture.label: Interactive executive experience
architecture.detail: Guided and explorer modes on one route registry, built from validated source data.

valueModel.question: What does one finished, evidenced and approved piece of work cost, all in?
valueModel.signal: Falls as shared capabilities are reused across modules.

valueModel.question: How long does a process or policy change take to reach the people doing the work?
valueModel.signal: Measured per module from request to release.

valueModel.question: How much net-new build does the next process need?
valueModel.signal: Should fall with each process cluster.

learned: An executive audience remembers one idea. Everything else belongs in the explorer.
Deriving the network from source data ended debates about whether the picture was right.
Writing the acceptance tests before the scenes kept the build honest about what was finished.
cases.scopeBoundary: Sanitised enterprise solution and experience blueprint using synthetic scenarios. Client identity, internal materials, and confidential implementation details are excluded. The case demonstrates Thomas's strategic framing, process architecture, operating-model design, technical blueprinting, and executive experience design.
limitations: A blueprint, not a deployed system. Nothing on this page has run on an organisation's real data.
The interactive build and its brief are private. This page describes them; it does not publish them.
The value lenses carry no numbers until a baseline exists in a real context.
The operating model and plan are illustrative and would need validation with the organisation.

cases.title: Enterprise AI Economics Simulator
cases.subtitle: An executive decision tool that turns a shared AI platform into one all-in annual figure, and shows which choices actually move it.
cases.problem: A risk division weighing a shared AI platform needs one all-in figure, not a token price: build, integration, hosting, dashboards, governance staff, licences and usage, and how the costs split when other functions share the platform.
cases.whyItMattered: At the illustrative defaults, fixed platform and governance costs are about 96 percent of year-one cost and tokens well under 1 percent. A business case built on token prices answers the wrong question.
constraints: No client data: illustrative list prices and placeholder benchmarks.
Runs as a static page in an executive conversation, with no account or data feed.
Every number has to be explainable and printable as a methodology.
cases.role: Product owner and model designer: problem framing, cost and benefit logic, scenario design and interface, with AI-assisted implementation that I reviewed and deployed.

contributions.detail: Which questions a division needs answered, for which use cases, and in which order.
Allocation across functions sharing the platform, a maturity ladder, hosting as a cost shape, governance staffing and a ten-year cash flow.
An interactive static tool with a printable calculation breakdown and its disclaimer.

decisions.title: Allocate the platform by the functions sharing it
decisions.rationale: The division pays one over the number of functions sharing the platform, shown next to a standalone figure, so the economics of sharing are visible.

decisions.title: Couple maturity to both build cost and efficiency
decisions.rationale: Higher maturity lowers the cost per request but raises build cost. The ladder makes that trade-off explicit instead of hiding it.

decisions.title: Select models by weighted criteria, not by vendor
decisions.rationale: Each task tier is scored on reasoning, speed, cost, context and safety, with a sovereignty bonus and a pool limited by the hosting choice.

decisions.title: Treat hosting as a cost shape
decisions.rationale: Cloud is priced per token, sovereign hosting adds a fixed commitment, and on-premise is a large fixed cost with a low marginal cost.

decisions.title: Make the methodology printable
decisions.rationale: Every figure is reproduced in a printable breakdown, so the numbers can be challenged line by line.

architecture.label: Context, scope and calibration
architecture.detail: Sector, country, staff, use cases, hosting and platform maturity.

architecture.label: Model selection per task tier
architecture.detail: Weighted scoring per complexity tier within the allowed model pool.

architecture.label: Cost per request and annual usage
architecture.detail: Tokens, caching, batching, retries and follow-ups.

architecture.label: Fixed costs
architecture.detail: Shared platform allocation, dashboards and governance staffing.

architecture.label: All-in annual cost
architecture.detail: Fixed costs plus licences plus usage, with the build amortised.

architecture.label: Ten-year cash flow and ROI
architecture.detail: Build spend, adoption ramp, growth and break-even.

valueModel.question: What does the division pay per year once platform, dashboards and governance are included?
valueModel.signal: Fixed costs are about 96 percent of year one at the illustrative defaults.

valueModel.question: How much does each extra function sharing the platform change the division's cost?
valueModel.signal: The division share falls as one over the number of functions.

valueModel.question: When does cumulative benefit overtake cumulative cost?
valueModel.signal: Year four at the illustrative defaults.

learned: The most useful finding was counter-intuitive: tokens barely move the number, while sharing and governance do.
Executives trust a model more when every assumption is visible and printable.
cases.scopeBoundary: Interactive prototype using illustrative planning assumptions and placeholder benchmarks. Not a client tool, a proposal or a production system.
limitations: Calibrated for a banking risk division only.
Benefits do not change with maturity level or hosting choice.
Placeholder prices and benchmarks, and no automated tests.
Opens behind an access-code page.

cases.title: DORA Article 12 AI Control Line
cases.subtitle: A working prototype that takes one regulatory obligation through guideline, control, infrastructure, verification, documentation and evidence, with human approval gates.
cases.problem: One obligation (DORA Article 12, geographically separate backups) has to become an updated guideline and control, an infrastructure change and its verification, a compliance-register update, documentation and an audit answer. Normally that is a manual hand-over chain across compliance, platform and product teams.
cases.whyItMattered: Every hand-over loses traceability. An auditor needs to see why a control changed, who approved it and which evidence supports it.
constraints: Synthetic fixtures only, with no real cloud or compliance-register access.
Runs locally on SQLite with no infrastructure.
AI output must be reviewable before it changes any artefact, and must fail visibly rather than invent output.
cases.role: Workflow architect and product owner: regulatory framing, state-machine and approval design, model assignment, verification and evidence design, with AI-assisted implementation that I reviewed and tested.

contributions.detail: Turning one article into a chain of reviewable artefacts.
An explicit transition table with reject paths and three human gates.
Deterministic policy checks and a content-hash provenance log linked to approvals.

decisions.title: An explicit transition table with reject paths
decisions.rationale: Every state change, including a rejection back to the previous state, is declared in one table, so the workflow can be tested and audited.

decisions.title: Assign models by task
decisions.rationale: Regulatory reasoning, infrastructure proposals and documentation have different cost and quality needs, so each task has its own model behind one provider interface.

decisions.title: No silent fallback
decisions.rationale: Without a model key the workflow stops with an error rather than producing plausible placeholder output.

decisions.title: Deterministic verification, not model judgement
decisions.rationale: Proposed infrastructure is checked by policy-as-code rules before a human reviews it.

decisions.title: Provenance on every file transformation
decisions.rationale: Source and target hashes are linked to approval and correlation identifiers, and a compliant status requires evidence.

architecture.label: Source fixtures
architecture.detail: Regulatory text, guideline, controls and infrastructure configuration, all synthetic.

architecture.label: AI proposal layer
architecture.detail: Guideline, control, infrastructure and documentation proposals.

architecture.label: State machine with three human gates
architecture.detail: Explicit transitions, reject paths and approval records.

architecture.label: Policy verification
architecture.detail: Deterministic rule checks before review.

architecture.label: Infrastructure write and deployment
architecture.detail: Simulated, not connected to a cloud account.

architecture.label: Documentation and evidence manifest
architecture.detail: Generated documents, provenance log and an audit response.

valueModel.question: How long does one obligation take from input to evidence?
valueModel.signal: Seeded workshop estimates of 74 hours manual against 17 assisted, labelled illustrative in the repository.

valueModel.question: Can each artefact be traced to its input and approval?
valueModel.signal: Hash-linked provenance for each file transformation.

learned: Approval gates only help when the reviewer sees a verified proposal rather than a draft to proofread.
Failing loudly without a model key was worth more than a graceful fallback.
cases.scopeBoundary: Working prototype on synthetic fixtures. Cloud, deployment and register integrations are simulated. Client context is excluded.
limitations: Deployment, cloud and register integrations are simulated.
Approvals are not authenticated, and some routes bypass the gates.
Only one model provider is implemented behind the abstraction.
Unit tests only (112 cases), with no end-to-end tests or CI; the audit trail can be reset.

cases.title: Enterprise NFR Agent Platform
cases.subtitle: Eighteen NFR domain agents on one orchestrator, sharing a run lifecycle, an approval step, a write-back path and an audit record.
cases.problem: NFR work spans service-management records, control and policy registers, regulatory publications and analyst judgement, and is usually handled one domain at a time.
cases.whyItMattered: When every domain builds its own agent, the control plumbing is rebuilt each time. A shared lifecycle turns each new domain into mostly prompts and data.
constraints: Synthetic data only, with no client systems.
Consequential writes to a system of record wait for a named role.
Runs locally, with every model call observable.
cases.role: Platform architect: orchestration model, approval and write-back design, knowledge graph and observability, with AI-assisted implementation that I reviewed and deployed.

contributions.detail: One orchestrator and step taxonomy for 18 domain agents, so interface, audit and scheduling are built once.
Role-restricted approval with a fail-safe timeout, typed write-back to a ServiceNow developer instance and a follow-up outcome check.
An OpenAI-compatible gateway with retries, metrics and tracing, covered by 48 tests.

decisions.title: One orchestrator for every domain agent
decisions.rationale: All agents share one step taxonomy and run lifecycle, so the interface, audit and scheduling are built once.

decisions.title: Approval as a blocking step with a fail-safe
decisions.rationale: Decisions are restricted by role, and no decision or a timeout means no write-back.

decisions.title: Write-back as typed, re-checked actions
decisions.rationale: Each write is recorded on its step and checked again later to confirm the outcome.

decisions.title: A shared graph, continuously enriched
decisions.rationale: Service-management records and the record pipeline feed one entity graph that all domains can use.

decisions.title: One model client with ordered fallback
decisions.rationale: Model access goes through a single client, with an optional gateway for metrics and tracing.

architecture.label: Sources
architecture.detail: A ServiceNow developer instance, synthetic registers and public feeds.

architecture.label: Knowledge graph
architecture.detail: An entity graph enriched from records and documents.

architecture.label: Agent layer
architecture.detail: 18 domain agents, run as direct chains or orchestrated runs.

architecture.label: Approval step
architecture.detail: Role-gated decisions with a timeout and a notification.

architecture.label: Write-back and outcome checks
architecture.detail: Typed actions against the service-management API, re-checked later.

architecture.label: Inference gateway
architecture.detail: Metrics, tracing and retries for every model call.

valueModel.question: What does the next NFR domain cost to add?
valueModel.signal: Mostly prompts and data: lifecycle, approval, write-back and audit are shared.

valueModel.question: Which writes wait for a human today?
valueModel.signal: Approval is active in 5 of 18 workflows; extending it is the next step.

learned: The platform question is about a shared lifecycle and controls, not the number of agents.
A graph only pays off when the agents query it, and that wiring comes next.
cases.scopeBoundary: Prototype on synthetic data and a ServiceNow developer instance. No client data or credentials. Not a production deployment.
limitations: Approval is active in 5 of 18 workflows, and one self-resolve path writes without approval.
Approver identity and decisions are not yet stored durably.
The domain agents do not yet query the knowledge graph.
The backend has no tests and is not packaged for deployment.

cases.title: AIRLOCK Regulated AI Workload Foundry
cases.subtitle: A pattern for auditable, policy-gated AI workloads, runnable locally, with the AWS layer kept as unapplied reference architecture.
cases.problem: Regulated firms need AI-assisted recommendations where every figure can be traced, tools are restricted by policy and a named person approves before anything is released. Rebuilding those controls for every pilot is slow.
cases.whyItMattered: A proof of concept rarely says how it would be evaluated, approved and released. Making those steps reusable is what turns a demonstration into a platform.
constraints: Synthetic data only, with no cloud credentials or spend.
No claim of regulatory compliance.
The model must never produce financial figures.
EU data residency by default.
cases.role: Pattern designer: workflow, policy and approval design, the finance-engine boundary and the reference architecture, with AI-assisted implementation that I reviewed.

contributions.detail: A 12-stage workflow with policy-gated tools and approval records, runnable locally.
Figures come from a decimal engine and are hashed; the model only narrates.
Ten Terraform modules for a controlled AWS deployment, never planned or applied.

decisions.title: A deterministic engine; the model only narrates
decisions.rationale: Financial figures come from a decimal calculation engine and each result is hashed, so no figure depends on model output.

decisions.title: A local mode behind one switch
decisions.rationale: A scripted adapter runs the whole pattern offline at no cost, with a switch to a cloud model adapter.

decisions.title: Policy-gated tools
decisions.rationale: A hard deny on external sends, per-stage tool permissions, and export only after approval.

decisions.title: A modular monolith with workload-agnostic packages
decisions.rationale: Policy, evidence, finance, adapter and evaluation packages can serve the next workload.

decisions.title: Write down what is built and what is reference
decisions.rationale: A claims ledger and an implementation-status matrix separate the runnable part from the reference architecture.

architecture.label: Interface and API
architecture.detail: A React interface over API routes with background runs.

architecture.label: 12-stage workflow
architecture.detail: Staged state machine with an approval pause.

architecture.label: Shared packages
architecture.detail: Policy, evidence, finance, adapter and evaluations.

architecture.label: Run and approval records
architecture.detail: Persisted locally on SQLite.

architecture.label: Model adapter
architecture.detail: Scripted locally; the cloud adapter is a stub.

architecture.label: AWS reference layer
architecture.detail: Ten Terraform modules, never planned or applied.

valueModel.question: How quickly can the next workload reach an evaluated, approved release?
valueModel.signal: Reuse of the policy, evidence, approval and evaluation packages.

valueModel.question: Can every figure and every action be traced?
valueModel.signal: Hashed finance results and evidence-grounded outputs.

learned: Writing down what is reference architecture made the implemented part more credible, not less.
Keeping the model away from the numbers removed a whole class of review risk.
cases.scopeBoundary: Local prototype on synthetic data with a scripted model. The AWS and Terraform layer is reference architecture that has never been applied. No compliance claim.
limitations: Scripted model only; the cloud model adapter is a stub.
A single approval step without authentication, mutable approval records and a release gate that does not yet block.
One workload; the second is a placeholder.
The Terraform has never been planned or applied, and CI currently fails.

cases.title: Regulatory reporting and data transformation
cases.subtitle: Anonymised professional delivery: a FINMA reporting and data-adequacy programme on a Databricks data platform.
cases.problem: A Swiss insurer needed regulatory reporting and data adequacy that would meet FINMA expectations, which depends on data that is complete, traceable and produced the same way every cycle.
cases.whyItMattered: Regulatory reporting recurs and is examined. A governed data platform makes each cycle repeatable and easier to evidence than manual assembly.
constraints: Regulatory expectations set the scope and the timeline.
Risk, data and technology workstreams had to move together.
Client identity, data and reporting content stay confidential.
cases.role: Originated the programme and held end-to-end delivery responsibility: execution, regulatory compliance, and coordination across risk, data and technology workstreams.

contributions.detail: Originated the programme.
End-to-end delivery responsibility across workstreams.
Platform implementation delivered within the programme.

decisions.title: Treat reporting and data adequacy as one programme
decisions.rationale: Reporting quality depends on data adequacy, so both were delivered in one framework.

decisions.title: Deliver on a shared data platform
decisions.rationale: A platform implementation, rather than report-by-report fixes, supports every future reporting cycle.

architecture.label: Source data
architecture.detail: Insurer data feeding the reporting process.

architecture.label: Databricks data platform
architecture.detail: Implemented within the programme.

architecture.label: Data adequacy
architecture.detail: Completeness and quality against the reporting framework.

architecture.label: FINMA reporting
architecture.detail: Regulatory reporting outputs.

valueModel.question: Can each reporting cycle run the same way and be evidenced?
Does the data meet the adequacy expectations?

learned: Data adequacy is an operating discipline, not a one-off clean-up.
cases.scopeBoundary: Anonymised professional delivery. No client name, data, reporting content or results are published. Further detail is available in conversation.
limitations: Anonymised: the client and its results cannot be shown.
Adoption and value detail is shared in conversation, not on this site.
